other_side: Zitron's case cuts underneath the whole model-ownership debate: to him it is a rounding error beside the fact that enterprise AI has no measurable return. He argues the boom rests not on ROI but on "vibes" and a "cult-like psychosis," and that no architectural choice — open weights, fine-tuning, closed tuning — changes the economics, because "without OpenAI, the AI industry doesn't exist." He notes API costs already "became a 'huge issue'" for enterprise customers, and that four years in there is still no agreed accounting of what these models actually cost to run. He would read Inkling and Microsoft Frontier Tuning not as sovereignty on offer but as fresh ways to keep spending on something that has not shown a return.
truth_beneath: The single variable both men orbit is enterprise AI economics — whether the cost of running these models is ever justified by the value enterprises get back. Both accept the same facts: token costs are large and real, and the unit economics are genuinely murky. The empirical question that will resolve is whether enterprises running fine-tuned or open-weights stacks show durable, auditable ROI; the observable that settles it is published enterprise unit economics and renewal data — does cost-per-outcome fall and does spend keep being renewed? The residue is pure worldview: NLW sees an experimental period with alpha for nimble teams, Zitron sees a capital misallocation heading for collapse. NLW is vindicated if fine-tuning lowers cost-per-outcome and enterprises keep paying and expanding; Zitron if spend keeps climbing while returns don't and a major player runs out of money. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom to an audience of buyers, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype to subscribers who reward it — so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: enterprise token cost is a real, unsolved problem. Watch whether any enterprise publishes hard fine-tuning ROI numbers, or whether the bills just keep rising.
